r1: Switch to Dual Rope Cable Pullover (neutral grip)
why: Full overhead flexion with internal rotation narrows the space under the acromion. Cut the top range first, then swap the long-lever pattern for a short-lever pull.
Grip is what irritates elbow and wrist tendons. Straps take the forearm out of it while the back still gets the work.
A heavy DB at end-range overhead is the likely uncomfortable for a rotator cuff. A neutral grip DB Row will be more appropriate
Rack pulls help pre-create tension in the back to prevent too much form breakdown/spinal flexion

r1: Raised deadlift (bar on stacked plates, mid-shin)
why: Deep hip flexion at the bottom is what pinches an irritated hip. Raising the bar cuts the flexion angle; the hip thrust trains the same muscles with the hip barely flexed.

r2: Ensure elbows are locked out and grip is being hooked onto the bar, not squeezing
why: Mixed grip loads the supinated arm's biceps tendon, heavy grip loads the forearm. Straps take the grip out
A more upright angle cuts the load. The TRX helps maintain neutral elbow position to reduce shoulder stress
A fixed bar locks the wrist and forearm into one position. TRX let them rotate freely. If that still hurts, go light and slow on the DB Row
Wide overhand plus full stretch at the top is the aggravating combo. Neutral grip and trimming the top range first, then remove overhead entirely.

r2: SA Lat pulldown, D handle, lighter, 3-sec lowering
why: Straps offload the grip. Slow, controlled loading is what tendons tolerate and adapt to best.
Neutral grip keeps the shoulder in a friendlier rotation. The DB Row lets you pick a load that isn't your whole bodyweight.
Pull ups are a common elbow irritant. The foot assistance takes some of your bodyweight off; the TRX Row allows a neutral position which should help
The unsupported, rotated hinge position is what bothers the back. Chest support removes the spinal demand completely.

r1: Reduced range: elbow tucked, stop at torso line, lighter
r2: Band row, neutral grip, elbow tucked
why: Pulling the elbow way past the torso drives the shoulder forward. Shorten the range, then move to a band, which gets lighter at the start of the pull.
Take the grip demand out and the back work stays exactly the same.

r1: Move slightly further back to prevent reaching overhead
why: Same logic as the bilateral pulldown. Cut the stretched overhead start, then take the arm out of overhead completely.
A bent-over row asks the back to hold an isometric hinge under load. Support the chest and that demand is gone.
Wide flared elbows put more stress through the front of the shoulder. Tuck and neutralise first.

r1: More upright body angle, neutral grip
why: Body angle is the load dial on TRX. Stand taller before changing the exercise.
Less load through the grip. Light, higher-rep work keeps the tendon loaded without flaring it.
Flared elbows with overhead arms are a common impingement position. Tuck the elbows first, then move the arms below shoulder height.

r2: Think 'punch the sky' Keep weight through the heel of the hand (Safely)
why: Neutral grip stacks the wrist over the forearm. Holding the bar end keeps the wrist straight, and the angle is lighter.
The stretched bottom of a fly with a long lever arm is tough on the front of the shoulder. The floor caps the range; the press shortens the lever.
A long lever puts a big load on the inner elbow. Bending the arms shortens it; the press takes it away.
A barbell fixes your hands. DBs let the shoulder find its own path; neutral grip plus the floor cuts rotation and bottom-end stretch.

r1: Wrists stacked, bar in heel of the hand
why: Most bench wrist pain is the bar sitting in the fingers and bending the wrist back. Fix the position before swapping.
A fixed bar can force the elbows into a position they don't like. DBs free it up; the floor caps the range and neutral grip eases the elbow.
Neutral grip reduces the internal rotation at the bottom. The floor then caps the range.

r1: Keep weight in the heel of the hand, think 'punch the sky'
why: Neutral grip lets the wrist sit in line with the forearm.
The steeper the incline, the more the press becomes overhead. Drop the angle first, then go flat.
Incline reduces the % of bodyweight you press. The floor press gives full control of load and range.
Flat hands force the wrist into full extension under load. Handles keep it straight.
The landmine's angled path avoids end-range overhead. If that still bites, move to a flat press with neutral grip.
Standing OHP invites lower back arching to get the bar overhead. A backrest stops it; half-kneeling locks the pelvis.
The barbell holds the wrist in extension. Neutral grip, then a lower angle.
Overhead position is usually the problem with cuff pain. Move to a flat press, then neutral grip to reduce rotation further.

r1: Seated DB press, back supported, neutral grip
why: Stops the lower back arching to compensate for overhead range.
Neutral grip keeps the forearm in a friendlier position; the landmine lowers the load.
The landmine is already a shoulder-friendly option. If it still hurts, move the press further away from overhead.
Half-kneeling with a glute squeeze locks the pelvis and stops overextension.
Raising in the scapular plane with thumbs up opens space under the acromion. Isometrics let you load a grumpy tendon with less pain.
The overhead finish is the aggravating part. Keep the external rotation work, which is exactly what the cuff wants.

r1: Drop the Y: T + W only, chest supported on incline
why: The Y position is the most overhead. Cut it, then drop below shoulder height.

r1: DB RDL, stop at the knee
why: Less load, shorter lever and shorter range

r1: DB RDL, stop at the knee
why: Cutting the range limits how deep into hip flexion you go, which is what pinches. The hip thrust trains the same muscles with barely any flexion.

r1: Goblet squat to box (at or above parallel)
why: Knee load rises with depth (Escamilla 2001). A box sets the range; the Spanish squat is a staple for patellar pain.
The SSB keeps you more upright than a straight bar, which cuts spinal shear. Goblet squats drop the load right down and keep you upright too.
Deep flexion pinches. A wider stance and toes out give the hip room; a box stops you going too deep.
Low bar or back squat demands a lot of external rotation. The safety bar or front-loading removes that.

r1: Maintain Neutral Spine, don't let hips move independently from spine
why: The floor bridge has less range for the lower back to overextend into.

r1: Split squat (rear foot on floor), reduced range
why: Rear foot elevation drives more load into the front knee. Flatten it out, then load it isometrically.
The rear hip gets a big hip flexor stretch under load. Lower the foot, then take the stretch out.
Remove the extra depth, then remove the stepping.
The deficit is what takes the hip into deep flexion. Remove it first.

r1: Reduce range to knee height, 3-sec lowering
why: Shorter range means a shorter lever on the spine; slow lowering means control over the flaring end range.
Less hip flexion at the bottom, then remove flexion entirely.
Front-foot elevation increases depth and knee travel. Flatten, then isometric.
Longer lever with feet on the bench. Bring the feet back in to shorten it.

r1: Lateral lunge to a box (reduced depth)
why: The box controls depth; the goblet squat removes the lateral shift.
Groin and inner hip issues hate the big stretched lunge. Reduce it, then use a low-range abductor exercise.
Static split squats remove the deceleration demand. Isometrics are well tolerated with patellar tendon pain (Rio 2015).
Shorter stance means less hip flexor stretch on the back leg.
Removing the balance demand stops the back from compensating.
Staggered stance keeps it unilateral but reduces the hip stability demand.

r1: Reduced range (to a block under the back knee)
why: A pad controls depth; the isometric keeps the knee loaded without the pain-provoking movement.
Less hip flexor stretch on the back leg.

r1: Lower box (knee above 90° at the top)
why: A lower box means less knee flexion under load. If it still hurts, use an isometric.
Heel elevation drives more knee forward = more patellar load. Flatten the feet and cap the depth.
Split the load across both legs, then hold. Load the Achilles, don't skip it: tendons respond to load (Silbernagel 2007).
Box height is the load dial. Go higher first, then use both legs.
Already a knee rehab staple. Reduce depth, then hold still.
Isometrics reduce patellar tendon pain in the short term. The band lets you sit back and take load off the front of the knee.
Remove the forward braking force, then remove the stepping.
Less stride length means less hip flexor stretch and hip flexion demand.
Less knee bend means less patellofemoral compression. The band shifts the load away from the front of the knee.
Loaded flexion and rotation is a lower back irritant. Remove the rotation, then work anti-extension.
Same core demand, lying on your back.
Dead bugs remove lumbar flexion

r2: Dead bug hold (arms and legs at 90°)
why: A shorter lever, then hold.
Shorter levers mean less extension pull on the lower back.
A shorter lever means less shoulder demand.
Less load through the supporting arm.
A wider base means less rotational demand.
Loaded flexion plus rotation is one of the worst combos for an irritated back. Swap to controlled rotation, then anti-rotation.
Less load through the shoulder, then an anti-lateral flexion exercise with no shoulder load.
Keep the anti-lateral flexion, lose the grip.
Asymmetric load can flare a sensitive back. Balance it out, then go lighter.
Neutral grip reduces distal biceps stress. Isometrics load the tendon with less pain.
A straight bar forces full supination. Neutral grip lets the wrist sit naturally; the isometric hold loads the arm with no movement at the wrist.

r1: Preacher curl over an incline bench
why: Front-of-shoulder pain can come from the long head of biceps. A preacher curl reduces its stretch.
Deep elbow flexion under load is what irritates the triceps tendon. Pushdowns reduce it; a close press trains triceps with far less elbow stress.
Slow, controlled loading, then isometric.
A flat bar locks the wrists. A rope lets them sit naturally.
Freer wrist and forearm position, then isometric.
Heavy grip loads the forearm tendons. Go lighter and slower, then use an isometric hold.

r2: Preacher curl over an incline bench
why: Incline curls put the long head of biceps into a big stretch. Take it out.
The stretched bottom position is where distal biceps stress peaks.

r1: Stop short of full lockout at the bottom
why: The bottom of a preacher curl is peak strain for the distal biceps tendon
A pronated lowering loads the forearm extensors (tennis elbow territory). Remove the pronation.
Lower the landing forces first, then keep the power work with no landing at all.
The Achilles takes a lot of load on take-off and landing. Reduce it, then keep the power work without leaving the floor.

r1: Hands on DBs or a bench
why: Neutral wrist and less bodyweight through the hands.
A box reduces the flexed-spine pickup. The carry keeps the hug position without the lift.

r1: D Ball to chest (no shoulder finish)
why: The shoulder load is at the top. Stop at the chest.
Remove the ballistic end, then remove flexion.
Remove the overhead throw first.
Cap the depth
